intro: Four old trees stand in four villages of the Münsterland, the flat farm country around Münster, between 14 and 34 kilometres from the city and best reached by bike or car. Start with the Kopfulme in der Beerlage near Billerbeck, a hollow pollarded white elm of roughly 350 years that you can step inside. The other three are limes with court history: the split Dicke Linde of Asbeck, more than ten metres round, Altenberge's coat-of-arms Krüsellinde, and the Heidenbaum at Laer, what is left of an old county's court lime.
meta_description: Four old trees across the Münsterland countryside: a hollow 350-year-old elm you can stand inside, and three limes where courts once sat.
question_answer: The oldest tree we map in the Münsterland is the Dicke Linde of Asbeck, a split large-leaved lime on Lindenweg at the edge of Asbeck in Legden, put at about 500 years by the tree register and about 600 by the municipality. The Heidenbaum at Laer carries the same claim of over 500 years, but that figure is tradition rather than measurement, and only a remnant of that tree still stands.
question_meta: The Dicke Linde of Asbeck in Legden, a split lime 10.47 metres round, is 500 to 600 years old depending on the source.
question_context: Nobody has cored any of these four trees, so every age here is an estimate, and two of them disagree with themselves. The Dicke Linde's century of uncertainty comes from two honest sources: a tree register that measured it in September 2022 and wrote 500 years, and the municipality of Legden, which says about 600. Its girth of 10.47 metres does not settle the matter, because lightning split the trunk and the figure may take in two stems grown together. Since the 1980s steel rods and wire ropes have kept it standing. The Heidenbaum at Laer is the other contender, the court lime of the old free county, with a sandstone cross beneath it; what survives is a reduced trunk 4.06 metres round, and its age of over 500 years is what the village has always said rather than anything measured. The best-loved tree of the four is younger: the Kopfulme in der Beerlage near Billerbeck, a hollow pollarded elm of roughly 350 years. Asbeck lies in the west of the region with no railway, so plan on a bike or a car.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in the Münsterland?
faq.a: The Dicke Linde of Asbeck in Legden, a split large-leaved lime 10.47 metres round, at about 500 years by the tree register and about 600 by the municipality. The Heidenbaum at Laer is claimed to be over 500 too, but only a remnant stands and its age is tradition rather than measurement.

faq.q: Can you really stand inside the Kopfulme?
faq.a: Yes. The trunk of the Kopfulme in der Beerlage is completely hollow with an opening you can step into, and the elm is alive around it. It stands beside a signed footpath on the Steinfurter Aa, about five kilometres from Billerbeck station.

faq.q: How do I get to these trees?
faq.a: By bike or car. The four stand in four villages, Billerbeck, Legden, Altenberge and Laer, between 14 and 34 kilometres from Münster. Only Billerbeck has a railway station, on the RB63 from Münster, about 30 minutes, and even from there the Kopfulme is a five-kilometre ride.

Yes, all four. Each is a protected natural monument on public ground: the Kopfulme by a footpath, the Dicke Linde on a village street in Asbeck, the Krüsellinde beside a wayside chapel in Altenberge, and the Heidenbaum by the street Am Heidenbaum in Laer.

trees.name: The Kopfulme in der Beerlage

location.address: Beerlage, Bauerschaft of Billerbeck (Kreis Coesfeld), by the Steinfurter Aa, Landschaftsplan Baumberge-Nord

trees.access: Free. Naturdenkmal (Kreis Coesfeld, ND BI 02) beside a signed foot path, public ground; the elm stands at the Steinfurter Aa. Register: 'oeffentlich zugaenglich'.
trees.transport: About 5 km from Billerbeck station (RB63 from Muenster, ~30 min); no timetable verified for the last stretch, a bike or car is the realistic way.
trees.story:
You can stand inside this elm. The trunk of the Kopfulme in der Beerlage is hollow all the way through, with an opening you can step into, and the tree is still alive around you.

Kopfulme means head-pollard elm. For generations this European white elm was cut back to a stubby head, the old way of taking wood from a tree without felling it, and that is why it grew short and wide rather than tall: 5.56 metres round when it was last measured in 2020, and only about twelve metres high. The bark has swallowed the remains of an old pasture fence, so the tree carries its working life on its skin.

How old it is depends on the source. The tree register that follows it says about 300 years. A 2011 profile put its planting near 1650, give or take seventy years, which, if that date holds, puts it in the ground within a lifetime of the Thirty Years' War. Roughly 350 is the honest middle, and the band is wide on purpose.

It stands beside a signed footpath on the Steinfurter Aa, outside Billerbeck, protected as a natural monument by the Coesfeld district. The crown sits low and needs cutting back again, which for a pollard is less a threat than a return to habit. One of the people who keeps a German tree register calls it his favourite tree of all. Step inside and you will understand him.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the short, completely hollow trunk with an opening you can step into, 5.56 metres round. It stands right beside the signed footpath along the Steinfurter Aa in the Beerlage.

trees.name: The Dicke Linde of Asbeck

location.address: Lindenweg / Auf der Horst, Asbeck, Legden (Kreis Borken)

trees.access: Free. Stands on the edge of the village at Lindenweg, a paved living street; Naturdenkmal, open to anyone.
trees.transport: Asbeck is in Legden, about 13 km west of Billerbeck; no rail. Bus links not verified, car or bike realistic.
trees.story:
The Dicke Linde of Asbeck measures 10.47 metres round, and part of the reason is that it is no longer one trunk. Lightning split this large-leaved lime and left a big hollow in it. What stands now is a split trunk, possibly two stems grown together, so the figure measures all of it rather than a single bole. Either way it is the thickest tree on this page by a wide margin.

Since the 1980s steel rods have held the trunk together and wire ropes have held up the crown, which still reaches about eighteen metres. The village has more than one name for it: the split lime, the court lime, the dance lime. Those names carry the stories. One says the Lords of Asbeck once laid a plank floor in its branches and held feasts up there; another says a free court sat beneath it. Both are tradition rather than record, and nobody has found the paperwork.

Its age is disputed by about a century. The tree register that measured it in 2022 says around 500 years. The municipality of Legden says about 600. Take the range.

A small wayside shrine showing Veronica with her veil stands under the tree, at the edge of the village on Lindenweg, a quiet residential street. Asbeck is in Legden, in the west of the Münsterland, with no railway; come by bike or car.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the split, hollow trunk held together with steel rods and the wire ropes in its crown. It stands at the edge of Asbeck on Lindenweg, with a small wayside shrine underneath.

best_time.label: June, when the old lime flowers and the street smells of it

trees.name: The Krüsellinde

location.address: Alter Muensterweg (40 m NW of house no. 47), Altenberge (Kreis Steinfurt)

trees.access: Free. In the Kruesel residential area on Alter Muensterweg with paved foot paths around it and a wayside shrine beside it; Naturdenkmal on public ground.
trees.transport: Altenberge is about 13 km east-north-east of Billerbeck, no rail; bus links not verified, car or bike realistic.
trees.story:
Altenberge put this lime on its coat of arms. The Krüsellinde is the village's heraldic tree, a large-leaved lime standing beside a wayside chapel on the Alter Münsterweg, the old road toward Münster, in what is now a residential quarter.

The spot is older in the record than the tree. Altenberge's own history says vehmic courts, the secretive Westphalian tribunals, were once held here, and that a rope and a sword still lie under the lime as symbols of that justice. The tree register adds a court table. The lime itself the register puts at about 280 years, so treat the courts and the tree as two facts about one place rather than as one story.

It is not a giant: 4.19 metres round in 2024 and about eighteen metres tall. What makes it worth looking at is the way the trunk breaks apart at around six metres into a crowd of separate stems, each one heading up on its own.

There is a caveat, and the register says it plainly. A tinder fungus is growing on the trunk. The tree was recorded as vital in October 2024, but this fungus feeds on wood, and a lime carrying it is a lime to visit sooner rather than later. If you have been recently and noticed a change, tell us.

Altenberge has no railway; a bike or a car is the realistic way out from Münster.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk that splits into many separate stems at about six metres, with a tinder fungus on the bark. It stands beside the wayside chapel on Alter Münsterweg, 40 metres north-west of house no. 47.

best_time.label: June, when the lime flowers above the wayside chapel

trees.name: The Heidenbaum

location.address: Am Heidenbaum / Darfelder Strasse (L 555), Laer (Kreis Steinfurt)

trees.access: Free. Stands on a small hill beside the public street Am Heidenbaum near the village edge, with the Heidenkreuz stone cross and a signboard; no entry needed.
trees.transport: Laer is about 9 km north-north-east of Billerbeck; no rail; bus links not verified, car or bike realistic.
trees.story:
What stands at the Heidenbaum today is the remnant of a court tree, and the ground still shows how big it once was. The tree register describes a reduced trunk left from the old lime, with traces of its former size visible in the soil around it. The survivor is 4.06 metres round and only about ten metres tall, small for a tree with this much history attached.

The history is the reason to come. This was the court lime of the old free county of Laer, whose court met "thor Lair thon synen Lynden", at Laer by its limes. The little hill it stands on served as a court and a burial place. Beneath the tree stands the Heidenkreuz, a cross of local Baumberge sandstone, said to recall the conversion of the region by the two Ewalds, the missionary brothers of the seventh century.

How much of that this particular tree has seen is the open question. The register says about 500 years and Laer's encyclopedia entry says over 500, but nobody has measured it, and a figure that round is closer to tradition than to dendrology. The register names it a large-leaved lime; no second source confirms the species.

It stands on public ground beside the street Am Heidenbaum at the edge of Laer, with a signboard explaining the site. If you know more about how old it really is, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the short, cut-back lime trunk with the Heidenkreuz sandstone cross standing directly beneath it. It stands on a small hill beside the street Am Heidenbaum, by a signboard.
